oneliner.t: Two-term Republican U.S. senator (since January 2015), former Alaska attorney general and natural resources commissioner, and retired Marine Corps Reserve colonel; he finished second in the Aug. 18, 2026 top-four primary (41.4%) behind Democrat Mary Peltola.

born.note: Wikipedia gives the date; the election pamphlet confirms the birthplace and age 61.

upbringing.t: Raised in Fairview Park, a Cleveland suburb, the son of Sandra and Thomas C. Sullivan. His father was president and CEO of RPM International, the coatings and chemicals company founded by his grandfather Frank C. Sullivan; his brother Frank C. Sullivan became RPM's CEO in 2002. He graduated from Culver Military Academy in Indiana in 1983, then Harvard (B.A. economics, 1987) and Georgetown (joint J.D./M.S. Foreign Service, 1993). He married Julie Fate, daughter of Fairbanks figures Hugh 'Bud' and Mary Jane Fate, in 1994; they have three daughters.

profile.office_years_note: U.S. Senate Jan 2015–present (~11.75 yrs) + Alaska Attorney General 2009–2010 + Alaska DNR Commissioner 2010–2013 + Senate-confirmed Assistant Secretary of State 2006–2009 (appointed). White House/NSC staff and Marine service not counted.

career.role: Marine Corps infantry officer (active 1993–97, 2004–06, early 2009, Afghanistan July 2013; Reserve from 1997; retired as colonel 2024)
career.org: U.S. Marine Corps / Marine Corps Reserve

career.role: Law clerk to Judge Andrew Kleinfeld
career.org: U.S. Court of Appeals, Ninth Circuit (Fairbanks)

career.role: Law clerk to Chief Justice Warren Matthews
White House Fellow; director, International Economics, NSC/NEC staff
Assistant Secretary of State for Economic, Energy and Business Affairs
Alaska Attorney General (appointed by Gov. Palin)
Commissioner of Natural Resources (appointed by Gov. Parnell)

platform.t: Says he has expanded oil and gas production in NPR-A, ANWR and Cook Inlet and advanced the Alaska LNG project to lower costs and create jobs.

Says he passed laws to strengthen salmon runs, reduce bycatch and ban imports of Russian and Chinese trawl-caught fish; in 2026 proposed a Bycatch Reduction Act requiring salmon excluders and tougher seafloor-contact accountability for trawlers.

Campaigns on what he calls the largest military and Coast Guard buildup in Alaska's history, including a $7 billion JBER recapitalization, four icebreakers homeported in Alaska and reopening the Adak Navy base.
Credits himself with tax cuts for families, small businesses and seniors and a $1.4 billion federal investment in Alaska's health system.
Strong supporter of Israel and an Iran hawk; lead cosponsor in 2025 of the U.S.-Israel Defense Partnership Act and the Enhanced Iran Sanctions Act.
Opposes abortion except in cases of rape, incest or a threat to the mother's life.

promises.t: Keep expanding Alaska oil and gas production and push the Alaska LNG project forward.
Pass his Bycatch Reduction Act (mandatory salmon excluders, seafloor-contact accountability, federal money for gear testing and electronic monitoring).
Continue the Alaska military and Coast Guard buildup (icebreakers, Adak, JBER).

claims.claim: Sworn in as Alaska's eighth U.S. senator on January 6, 2015, and re-elected in November 2020.

record.t: Senator since January 2015; beat Mark Begich in 2014 and Al Gross 54%–41% in 2020.

claims.claim: Serves on Armed Services, Commerce, Environment and Public Works, and Veterans' Affairs.

record.t: Wikipedia lists the same four committees, including chairmanship of the Armed Services readiness subcommittee.

claims.claim: UVA's Center for Effective Lawmaking ranks him among the Senate's top 10 most effective members.

record.t: The Center ranked him 8th among Senate Republicans in the 115th Congress and, per his own release, the most effective Republican senator on environment policy in the 116th. Neither source shows a top-10 rank among all senators.

claims.claim: Served over 30 years as a Marine Corps infantry officer and retired in early 2024 as a Reserve colonel.

record.t: Commissioned 1993, mostly in the Reserve after 1997 with active stints in 2004–06, 2009 and Afghanistan in 2013; retired in 2024 as a Reserve colonel.

claims.claim: Deployed to the Middle East, Afghanistan, and the Taiwan Strait and South China Sea.

record.t: A six-week Afghanistan deployment in July 2013 is documented, and the election pamphlet lists War on Terrorism Expeditionary and Afghanistan Campaign medals. No source reviewed documents the Taiwan Strait/South China Sea deployment.

claims.claim: Was Assistant Secretary of State, Alaska Attorney General and DNR Commissioner.

record.t: Assistant Secretary of State 2006–2009 (unanimously confirmed), Attorney General 2009–2010, DNR Commissioner 2010–2013.

claims.claim: Was a National Security Council director under Condoleezza Rice.

record.t: White House Fellow and NSC/NEC director 2002–2004. Rice was National Security Advisor then, not Secretary of State (she took that post in Jan. 2005), so the page’s title for her is inaccurate.

claims.claim: His Save Our Seas Act and Save Our Seas 2.0 Act were signed into law by President Trump.

record.t: He introduced SOS 2.0 in June 2019 and Trump signed it on Dec. 18, 2020; the original act was signed in October 2018 (sponsor not shown in the source). 'Most comprehensive in history' is characterization.

claims.claim: Harvard B.A. in economics; joint law degree and foreign-service master's from Georgetown.
Married to Julie Fate Sullivan for over 30 years, with three daughters.
Was massively outspent by national Democrats in both of his Senate races.

record.t: Total 2014 and 2020 outside spending on each side was not obtained (OpenSecrets is blocked to this tool; FEC IE tables did not load).

claims.claim: A Marine Corps Reserve colonel with 25 years of service and the only senator still serving in the military.

said.where: campaign Issues page, intro (claim #1 of sample)

record.t: Outdated text still on the live site: he retired from the Reserve in 2024, as his own 'Meet Dan' page says, so he is no longer serving.

said.where: campaign Issues page, item 8 of first section

record.t: Save Our Seas 2.0, which he sponsored, became law in December 2020.

claims.claim: Confirmed 218 federal judges, including two Supreme Court justices.

said.where: campaign Issues page, item 5 of first section

record.t: Judicial confirmation totals were not checked against Senate records. The count reflects a 2020-era page that has not been updated.

claims.claim: Mary Peltola voted against a pay raise for Alaska's troops.

said.where: Sullivan campaign TV ad (most-covered ad #1, per FactCheck.org)

record.t: She voted against the House's July 2023 NDAA over Republican amendments, then voted for the final compromise bill that kept the 5.2% raise. Sullivan voted for the same final bill.

claims.claim: Peltola had 'zero bills signed into law in two terms.'

said.where: remarks launching his campaign's anti-Peltola website (most-covered statement #2)

record.t: Congress.gov/GovTrack enactment counts for Peltola could not be reached. FactCheck.org notes one Peltola-cosponsored NDAA amendment became law, but that is not a bill she sponsored.

claims.claim: The Petersburg Dan J. Sullivan is a sham candidate working with Peltola and Democrats to confuse voters and 'rig' the election.

said.where: statements and NRSC letter (Alaska's News Source)

record.t: The only documented links are Dan J. Sullivan's use of Amber Lee, a consultant who has worked for Democrats, and small 2022/2024 ActBlue gifts to Peltola from 'a Dan Sullivan from Petersburg.' The elections director cited no evidence of coordination, a Superior Court judge ruled the Division of Elections’ new "good faith" test had no basis in law (he did not rule on coordination), and Peltola's campaign and the challenger deny it.

said.t: Hawkish pro-Israel, anti-Iran stance; lead cosponsor of the 2025 U.S.-Israel Defense Partnership Act.

did.t: Supported the 2024 supplemental aid package for Israel, Ukraine and other allies; earlier cosponsored the Israel Anti-Boycott Act (2017).

said.t: Election pamphlet says he passed legislation to reduce bycatch.

did.t: His Bycatch Reduction Act is described in August 2026 as a proposal, a reworked 2022 research task-force bill; no enacted bycatch law was identified in sources reviewed. Peltola and an Alaska Beacon commentary say he is among the trawl sector's top campaign-money recipients (no figures given).

said.t: Campaigns on support for troops and the Alaska military buildup.

did.t: Voted for the final FY2024 NDAA conference bill with the 5.2% pay raise.

evidence.t: He opposed the ACA and voted to repeal it; the law was not repealed. His campaign site now says he 'repeals negative aspects of Obamacare' (e.g., the Cadillac tax).

complicating.t: In December 2025 he was one of four Republicans voting to advance a Democratic bill extending enhanced ACA premium credits (per the AK key-vote pass); the dates of individual repeal votes were not pulled here.

promises_prev.promise: Build a road to the Ambler mining district (secure the right-of-way).

evidence.t: In June 2024 he added a rider to the FY2025 NDAA requiring BLM to grant the Ambler right-of-way; it was dropped from the final bill.

complicating.t: Later executive-branch actions on Ambler were not researched here.

entries.t: Withdrew support for Trump after the Access Hollywood tape.
Said he would vote for Trump; voted to acquit in both impeachment trials.
Endorsed second-term policies including DOGE spending cuts in his address to the Legislature; Trump endorsed his re-election (July 2025).
Has said 'the verdict is still out' on the human contribution to climate change.
Came out against Pebble after recordings suggested executives planned a larger mine.

statements.t: Lead cosponsor of the U.S.-Israel Defense Partnership Act and the Enhanced Iran Sanctions Act of 2025; has repeatedly urged direct retaliation against Iran over Houthi attacks and has visited Israel/the region at least three times since Oct. 7, 2023.

fec.committee: C00570994 (Alaskans for Dan Sullivan); leadership PAC True North PAC (C00571000)
fec.instate_note: Q1 2026 only: in-state donors were about 17% of his total (Alaska Public Media).
fec.src_note: Six-year election totals Jan 1, 2021–Jul 29, 2026. pac_all = FEC 'other committee contributions' (business, trade, ideological and leadership PACs combined; split not available). 'other' = $3,212,070.34 transfers from authorized committees (joint fundraising) + $311,524.48 other receipts + $9,375.85 offsets. The ~$250,000 AIPAC earmark in Q1 2026 sits inside itemized individual money. In Q1 2026 PACs gave about $277,000 (~24% of his quarter), mostly industry, trade, legal, lobbying and contractor PACs (Alaska Public Media).
fec.quarters_note: Q1 2026 reported as $1.7M (Alaska Public Media) or $2.1M (Straight Arrow News citing Politico); the two figures conflict and neither was checked against the filing.

support: Senate Leadership Fund — announced plans to spend $15M (planned, not confirmed as spent)
Last Frontier PAC (pro-Sullivan super PAC; anti-Peltola ads; amount not found)
oppose: Right For Alaska (super PAC, Hudson, Wis.) — ~$574,000 opposing him, Jul 30–Aug 7, 2026 (OpenSecrets). Its total spending in the race, including promoting Southworth and Heikes, was $2.2M by Aug 18 (NYT via Election Law Blog); FEC shows $2,353,093 in independent expenditures through Sep 30.
907 Initiative — more than $1M on negative ads and information campaigns featuring him (Alaska Public Media)

fec.outside_note: No FEC independent-expenditure totals for the race loaded (tables are script-rendered). Amounts above are from news reports at the dates given. Across the whole race, Alaska Public Media (Oct. 2, 2026) reports independent groups have spent more than $31 million since the Aug. 18 primary, about 70% on opposition; groups backing Sullivan have outspent groups backing Peltola by nearly $7 million.

corp.t: PAC money is a large share of his fundraising: $2,604,358 in other-committee contributions in the 2021–26 cycle, $2,462,069 in 2015–20 and $834,683 in 2014. Alaska Public Media found his Q1 2026 PAC money (~$277,000, about 24% of the quarter) came mostly from industry, trade, legal, lobbying and contractor PACs. A Peltola-campaign post and an Alaska Beacon commentary call him a top recipient of trawl-industry money, but neither gives a figure.

lobby.t: Pro-Israel money: Track AIPAC lists $789,874 in career donations from pro-Israel PACs (AIPAC, COPAC, NATPAC, RJC, NORPAC) and their large donors. AIPAC passed about $250,000 in earmarked contributions to him in Q1 2026 alone.

money2.note: Funders of Senate Leadership Fund and Last Frontier PAC (pro-Sullivan) were not obtained. Opposing groups: Right For Alaska's FEC summary (thru Sep 30, 2026) shows $2,375,017 raised — $1,285,000 from party committees and $990,000 from other committees (names not shown on the summary page) plus $100,000 from individuals (William Harris of Lexington, Mass., per OpenSecrets). 907 Initiative's funders were not found.

networth.note: No assets-minus-liabilities range was computed. The Alaska Current puts his reported assets at $4.1M–$12.3M; Quiver Quantitative (via Newsweek) estimates net worth near $8.4M. Largest asset: RPM International stock listed at $1M–$5M, plus a rental property up to $500,000.

trades.period: STOCK Act filings to Jan 2024 (Disclosed Capitol count; full range not shown)

note.t: The Alaska Current says he has sold about $800,000 of RPM stock in office, is the most active stock trader in the Alaska delegation, and reported some trades late (2018 and 2022). It reports trade timing; it does not document that he acted on non-public information. Peltola's campaign says he 'tripled his wealth'; the Alaska Current's review says trades roughly tripled his wealth. Senate eFD was not searched directly. He sold shares of RPM International, the coatings company his family has long been tied to, in Sept. 2018, Feb. 2020 (after a CDC briefing, about two weeks before pandemic shutdowns) and Nov. 2022 (a month before weak earnings). Reporting documents the timing, not any use of nonpublic information, and no committee of his directly oversees the company, so these sales are not counted as committee-overlap trades.

committees: Armed Services (chairs Readiness and Management Support subcommittee)
effectiveness.note: Sponsored/enacted counts not retrieved (congress.gov not reached). Enacted examples: Save Our Seas 2.0 (2020).

democracy.t: Voted against the objection to Arizona's electoral votes (objection failed 6–93).
Voted against the objection to Pennsylvania's electoral votes (failed 7–92).
Voted against creating an independent commission to investigate the Jan. 6 Capitol attack.

access.note: He took part in a fisheries debate in Kodiak with Peltola (described on Peltola's campaign site). He did not answer the Alaska Beacon voter-guide questionnaire. Totals for debates accepted/declined and town halls were not found.

note.t: Ohio native. Election pamphlet lists 29 years in Alaska: Fairbanks 1997–98, Anchorage 1998–2002 and 2009–present. In 2014, a tax assessor said he was a Maryland resident during his State Department years, when he claimed Bethesda as his primary residence but voted absentee in Alaska.

checks.legal: No CourtListener/Justia searches were run (not reached this pass). Senate Ethics Committee site not searched. News searches surfaced no lawsuits or charges against him. The only legal/compliance item found is late STOCK Act transaction reports (2018, 2022), per the Alaska Current.
checks.foreign: Senate eFD not searched directly; news coverage of his disclosures (Newsweek, Alaska Current) mentions no foreign assets. FARA not searched. No foreign-government or foreign-business ties surfaced.
checks.claims: Mechanical sample: (a) every checkable claim on the campaign 'Meet Dan' page (dansullivanforalaska.com/meet-dan/): 11 rated (items on independent-voter share and his winning coalition are not checkable/opinion); (b) the first 10 items on the Issues page (first section 'Getting It Done in Washington'): intro claim (25 years/only serving senator) rated misleading, #8 ocean cleanup rated true, #5 judges unverifiable; #1 COVID, #2 ANWR/NPR-A, #3 '25% Obama cuts', #4 $300M water/sewer, #6 2A, #7 Green New Deal, #9 $50M public safety, #10 Alaska Native are opinion or were not checked. The Issues page appears to be largely 2020-era text. (c) Ad spend unknown; most-covered items: the campaign's 'pay raise' ad (FactCheck.org) and his Sept. 3, 2026 'zero bills' remarks. Also rated: his sham-candidate accusation against Dan J. Sullivan.
checks.democracy: 2021 certification objection votes (OnTheIssues, Senate Democrats floor record; Pennsylvania vote from the AK key-vote pass reading senate.gov); Wikipedia for the Jan. 6 commission vote. No search for 2020/2024 result statements beyond that.

legal.t: Filed periodic transaction reports late for two RPM stock trades from March and May 2018 (filed late July 2018); he said his managers did not tell him in time. The Alaska Current says he was also cited in 2022 for STOCK Act reporting violations, with the same explanation.
legal.status: Reported late; no penalty or ethics finding documented in sources reviewed

recordx.note: 'late' refers to STOCK Act transaction reports in 2018 and 2022, not annual reports (annual-report timeliness not checked). Missed-vote % not obtained (GovTrack not reached). FEC RFAI/notices tab did not load. The key-vote pass records him Not Voting on roll 119-2-252 (Sept. 29, 2026).

research_notes: RACE: Peltola led the certified Aug 18 primary 49.5% to 41.4% (Alaska Current/Beacon); the unofficial Aug 25 Division of Elections printout showed 48.22% to 42.64% with 99.5% of precincts. Recent polls are split (NYT/Siena Peltola +7; Quantus, Trafalgar, co/efficient Sullivan +1 to +2). FEC: three election views read directly (2014, 2020, 2026); 2026 figures run through Jul 29, 2026 (pre-primary). The candidate page does not show business vs. ideological PAC splits, and OpenSecrets is blocked. AIPAC earmark figure covers only Q1 2026. CLAIMS: the Issues page still contains 2020-era COVID and judge-count text; the 'only senator still serving' line is outdated given his 2024 retirement. The NRSC/Sullivan accusation that Dan J. Sullivan is a Peltola-coordinated plant is not supported by documents reviewed; an FEC complaint by Americans for Public Trust (Sept 2026) alleges coordination between Dan J. Sullivan and the 907 Initiative, not with Peltola. FINANCES: the RPM–EPW overlap is an inference from EPW's environmental-regulation jurisdiction; trade timing relative to earnings comes from the Alaska Current's review, not a regulatory finding. Peltola's campaign figure that he 'made up to $2 million' trading conflates trade volume with gains (the Alaska Current says an estimated $2 million in trades). RELATIVES: RPM International is run by his brother; its corporate record is not his.
